title: The Imperfect: When I Was Little
bigQuestion: How does Spanish let you paint a picture of the past, not just list what happened?

story.title: The Town with the Blue Doors
story.kicker: A grandmother in Chicago remembers her childhood town in Michoacán, one habit at a time.
paragraphs: Every Sunday, Daniela visits her grandmother in Little Village. This week Daniela has homework for Spanish class: interview an older relative about their childhood. She sets her phone on the kitchen table and presses record. Her grandmother, Abuela Rosa, smiles and pours two cups of hot chocolate. "¿Qué quieres saber?" (What do you want to know?) she asks.

"¿Cómo era tu pueblo?" (What was your town like?) Daniela asks. Abuela Rosa closes her eyes. "Mi pueblo era pequeño. Las casas tenían puertas azules. Había una plaza con una fuente." (My town was small. The houses had blue doors. There was a plaza with a fountain.) Daniela notices that every verb ends in -aba or -ía, or is a short word like era.

"¿Y qué hacías todos los días?" (And what did you do every day?) "Todas las mañanas, yo caminaba a la escuela con mis hermanos. Mi mamá hacía tortillas y mi papá trabajaba en el campo. Los domingos, íbamos al mercado." (Every morning, I walked to school with my brothers. My mom made tortillas and my dad worked in the fields. On Sundays, we went to the market.)

Daniela stops the recording. None of these sentences tells about one single moment. They tell what life was like, over and over, for years. "Abuela," she says, "your whole story is in the same tense." Her grandmother laughs. "Claro, mija. Así se cuentan los recuerdos." (Of course, sweetheart. That is how you tell memories.)
story.think: Abuela Rosa never says what happened on one specific day. Why do you think her memories use a different past tense than a story about one event?

lessons.title: The -aba Endings
lessons.mainIdea: Regular -ar verbs form the imperfect by dropping -ar and adding -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban.
reading: Picture Abuela Rosa saying, "Yo *caminaba* a la escuela" (I used to walk to school). The verb is caminar (to walk). To build the imperfect, drop the -ar to get the stem camin-. Then add the ending for the subject. For yo, the ending is -aba: caminaba. The imperfect is a past tense for actions that were ongoing, repeated or in the background.

Here is the full walk-through with hablar (to speak): yo hablaba, tú hablabas, él or ella hablaba, nosotros hablábamos, vosotros hablabais, ellos hablaban. Notice two things. First, the yo form and the él/ella form are the same: hablaba. Context or a subject pronoun tells you who. Second, only the nosotros form carries a written accent: hablábamos.

English speakers often forget the accent in hablábamos, or they put one where it does not belong, as in "hablába." Say the word aloud: ha-BLÁ-ba-mos. The stress falls on the third syllable from the end, so Spanish spelling needs the accent mark. Every regular -ar verb follows this pattern, including *trabajar* (to work) and *jugar* (to play), even though jugar changes its stem in the present. In the imperfect it is simply jugaba.

words.d: to walk — imperfect: caminaba, caminabas, caminaba, caminábamos, caminabais, caminaban
to work — imperfect: trabajaba (I/he/she used to work)
to play — no stem change in the imperfect: jugaba, jugábamos
the imperfect — a past tense for habits, descriptions and ongoing background actions

look.title: Walk Through Estudiar
look.text:
estudiar → drop -ar → estudi-
yo estudiaba
tú estudiabas
ella estudiaba
nosotros estudiábamos
vosotros estudiabais
ellos estudiaban
Ejemplo: De niña, mi prima estudiaba en Morelia. (As a girl, my cousin studied in Morelia.)
look.prompt: Now build the imperfect of bailar (to dance) for tú and for nosotros. Where does the accent go?

check.q: Which is the correct nosotros imperfect form of trabajar?
check.why: Nosotros adds -ábamos with a written accent. Trabajamos is present or preterite, and -íamos is for -er/-ir verbs.

check.q: "Mi abuelo ___ en el campo." Choose the imperfect of trabajar.
check.why: Mi abuelo is él, and the él imperfect ending for -ar verbs is -aba: trabajaba.

check.q: What is the imperfect tú form of jugar?
check.why: Jugar has no stem change in the imperfect, so it is jug- + -abas: jugabas. Jugabais is vosotros.

lessons.title: The -ía Endings
lessons.mainIdea: Regular -er and -ir verbs share one set of imperfect endings: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían.
reading: Abuela Rosa says, "Mi mamá *hacía* tortillas" (My mom made tortillas, again and again). The verb is hacer (to make or do). Drop the -er to get hac-, then add -ía. Even though hacer is irregular in the present and the preterite, it is regular in the imperfect. That is good news: almost every verb in Spanish is regular here.

The -er and -ir verbs share the exact same endings. Compare comer (to eat) and *vivir* (to live): comía, comías, comía, comíamos, comíais, comían; vivía, vivías, vivía, vivíamos, vivíais, vivían. Every form has an accent on the í. That accent breaks the i and the a into two syllables: vi-VÍ-a, not vi-VIA.

A common mistake is mixing the two families, as in "comaba" or "vivaba." Remember the rule by the vowel: -ar verbs keep an a sound (-aba), while -er and -ir verbs switch to í (-ía). Another mistake is dropping the accent. Without it, vivia looks like a different word and is misspelled. Verbs like *tener* (to have) and *salir* (to go out) follow the pattern too: tenía, salía.

words.d: to live — imperfect: vivía, vivías, vivía, vivíamos, vivíais, vivían
to make or do — regular in the imperfect: hacía
to have — imperfect: tenía (I/he/she had, used to have)
to go out or leave — imperfect: salía, salíamos

look.title: Two Families, One Pattern
look.text:
comer → com- → comía, comías, comía, comíamos, comíais, comían
escribir → escrib- → escribía, escribías, escribía, escribíamos, escribíais, escribían
Ejemplo: Cuando vivíamos en Uruapan, comíamos en casa de mi tía. (When we lived in Uruapan, we used to eat at my aunt's house.)
look.prompt: Write the imperfect of beber (to drink) for yo and of abrir (to open) for ellos.

check.q: Which is the correct imperfect ella form of vivir?
check.why: Vivir is an -ir verb, so it takes -ía with an accent: vivía. Vivaba mixes in the -ar ending, and vivia is missing the accent.

check.q: "Nosotros ___ mucho pan." Choose the imperfect of comer.
check.why: -er verbs take -íamos for nosotros, with an accent: comíamos.

check.q: Why is hacer easy in the imperfect?
choices: It is regular: hacía, hacías, hacía
check.why: Hacer is irregular in other tenses but regular in the imperfect: hac- + -ía.

lessons.title: Only Three Irregulars
lessons.mainIdea: Only ser, ir and ver are irregular in the imperfect: era, iba and veía.
reading: When Abuela Rosa says, "Mi pueblo *era* pequeño" (My town was small), she uses ser (to be). Ser does not follow the -ía pattern. Its imperfect forms are era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran. Notice that only éramos has an accent, just like hablábamos. The stress falls on the third syllable from the end.

The second irregular is *ir* (to go): iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban. It looks like an -ar verb even though ir is an -ir verb. "Los domingos, íbamos al mercado" means "On Sundays, we used to go to the market." The third irregular is *ver* (to see): veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían. Ver just keeps its e before the regular -ía ending.

That is the whole list. Spanish has dozens of irregular verbs in the preterite, but only three in the imperfect. Students sometimes invent forms like "seía" or "iría." Seía does not exist, and iría is the conditional (I would go), a different tense. When you see era, iba or veía, you know you are in the imperfect.

words.d: to be — imperfect: era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran
to go — imperfect: iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban
to see or watch — imperfect: veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían

look.title: Three Verbs in One Memory
look.text:
Abuela Rosa: "Yo era muy curiosa. Todos los sábados iba con mi papá al río. Allí veíamos garzas blancas."
(I was very curious. Every Saturday I used to go with my dad to the river. There we used to see white herons.)
look.prompt: Find the imperfect of ser, ir and ver in the memory. Then say one thing you used to see on the way to school.

check.q: Which is the imperfect nosotros form of ir?
check.why: Ir is irregular: íbamos, with an accent. Fuimos is preterite and iríamos is conditional.

check.q: "Cuando ___ niños, vivíamos en Pátzcuaro." Which form fits?
check.why: Ser in the imperfect for nosotros is éramos. Seíamos does not exist.

check.q: What does "Mis primos veían la tele" mean?
choices: My cousins watched a show once.
My cousins would watch TV if they could.
My cousins used to watch TV.
check.why: Veían is the imperfect of ver for ellos, so it describes a repeated past habit: used to watch.

lessons.title: Había: There Was, There Were
lessons.mainIdea: The imperfect of hay is había, which means both there was and there were.
reading: Abuela Rosa describes her plaza: "*Había* una fuente y había muchos árboles" (There was a fountain and there were many trees). In the present you say hay (there is, there are). In the imperfect, hay becomes había. It comes from the verb haber, and it is one of the most useful words for describing a scene.

English changes the verb for singular and plural: there was, there were. Spanish does not. Había stays the same no matter what follows: había un perro (there was a dog), había tres perros (there were three dogs). A very common error is "habían muchos árboles." Many native speakers say it, but standard Spanish uses the singular había.

Había is perfect for describing a *la plaza* (town square) or *el mercado* (the market) in a memory. "En el mercado había frutas, flores y música." (At the market there were fruits, flowers and music.) Once you have había, you can build a whole picture of a place, one detail at a time.

words.d: there was, there were — the imperfect of hay; it never changes for plural
the town square — the center of many Mexican and Latin American towns
the market — often open-air, with food, flowers and crafts
the fountain (also means source)

look.title: Paint the Plaza
look.text:
En el centro de mi pueblo había una plaza. En la plaza había una fuente vieja. Alrededor había bancos verdes y un quiosco. Por la tarde, siempre había niños jugando.
(In the center of my town there was a square. In the square there was an old fountain. Around it there were green benches and a bandstand. In the afternoon, there were always children playing.)
look.prompt: Use había three times to describe a place you remember from when you were younger.

check.q: "En mi escuela ___ muchos estudiantes." Which form is standard Spanish?
check.why: Había stays singular even before a plural noun in standard Spanish.

check.q: What does "Había un gato en la ventana" mean?
choices: There is a cat in the window.
There will be a cat in the window.
There was a cat in the window.
check.why: Había is the imperfect of hay: there was.

check.q: What is the present-tense form that había comes from?
check.why: Hay means there is or there are; its imperfect is había.

lessons.title: Used To and Would
lessons.mainIdea: The imperfect tells what someone used to do or would do again and again in the past.
reading: Think about something you did every summer when you were small. Maybe you went to the pool or visited a cousin. In English you might say "I used to swim" or "I would swim every day." In Spanish, one form covers both: nadaba. "Todos los veranos, nadaba en el lago." (Every summer, I used to swim in the lake.)

Words of repetition often travel with the imperfect. *Siempre* (always), todos los días (every day), cada domingo (every Sunday), *a menudo* (often) and *de vez en cuando* (from time to time) all signal a habit. "Mi papá siempre se levantaba a las cinco." (My dad always got up at five.) The habit happened many times, so Spanish uses the imperfect.

Be careful with English would. "I would go to the market" can mean a past habit (imperfect: iba) or something that depends on a condition (conditional: iría). Ask yourself: is this describing what used to happen? If yes, use the imperfect. English speakers who translate would word for word often write iría when they need iba.

words.d: always — a common clue for a repeated past habit
often — Íbamos al río a menudo. (We often went to the river.)
from time to time, once in a while
every day — signals a routine

look.title: A Week in Abuela's Childhood
look.text:
Los lunes, iba a la escuela a pie.
Los miércoles, ayudaba a mi mamá en la cocina.
Los sábados, jugaba fútbol con mis hermanos.
Los domingos, siempre íbamos a misa y después al mercado.
look.prompt: Write three sentences about your own weekly routine when you were eight, using the imperfect.

check.q: "When I was little, I would eat cereal every morning." Which verb fits?
check.why: This would describes a past habit, so Spanish uses the imperfect comía, not the conditional comería.

check.q: Which phrase signals a repeated habit?
check.why: De vez en cuando (from time to time) describes something that happened repeatedly.

check.q: What does "Siempre visitábamos a mis tíos" mean?
choices: We always used to visit my aunt and uncle.
We visited my aunt and uncle once.
We will always visit my aunt and uncle.
We would visit if we could.
check.why: Siempre plus the imperfect visitábamos describes a regular past habit.

lessons.title: Describing People and Places
lessons.mainIdea: Use the imperfect to describe how people, places and things were in the past.
reading: Imagine a photo of Abuela Rosa's house. It does not move, but it has details. "La casa era de adobe. Tenía un patio con macetas. La cocina olía a canela." (The house was made of adobe. It had a patio with flowerpots. The kitchen smelled of cinnamon.) Each verb describes how things were, so each is imperfect.

Physical and personality descriptions also go in the imperfect. "Mi abuelo era alto y *callado*. Llevaba un sombrero de paja." (My grandfather was tall and quiet. He wore a straw hat.) Use ser for traits: era alto. Use estar for conditions and locations: la casa estaba cerca del río (the house was near the river).

Students sometimes use the preterite for descriptions because it feels like "the" past tense: "La casa fue grande." That sentence sounds odd, as if the house was big for a set time and then stopped. For a description of how something was, choose the imperfect: la casa era grande. Words like *el patio* and *el adobe* help you build the setting.

words.d: quiet (person) — callada for a woman or girl
the courtyard or patio, often in the center of a house
adobe — sun-dried brick of earth and straw used in many older homes
to wear or carry — Llevaba un sombrero. (He wore a hat.)

look.title: Describe the Photo
look.text:
En la foto, mi abuela tenía diez años. Era delgada y tenía el pelo largo. Llevaba un vestido blanco. Estaba en la puerta de su casa y parecía contenta.
(In the photo, my grandmother was ten. She was thin and had long hair. She wore a white dress. She was at the door of her house and seemed happy.)
look.prompt: Describe an old photo of someone in your family in four imperfect sentences.

check.q: "Mi escuela ___ grande y moderna." Which verb best describes it in the past?
check.why: Describing what the school was like uses ser in the imperfect: era.

check.q: "La casa ___ cerca del río." Which verb fits?
check.why: Location uses estar, and a past description uses the imperfect: estaba.

check.q: What does "Mi abuelo llevaba un sombrero de paja" mean?
choices: My grandfather wore a straw hat.
My grandfather bought a straw hat.
My grandfather will wear a straw hat.
My grandfather took off his straw hat.
check.why: Llevaba is the imperfect of llevar (to wear), describing him.

lessons.title: Age, Time and Weather
lessons.mainIdea: Age, clock time and weather in the past are background facts, so they use the imperfect.
reading: "Cuando *tenía* siete años, aprendí a nadar." (When I was seven, I learned to swim.) In Spanish you have years, so age uses tener. Age in the past is a background fact, so it uses the imperfect: tenía. Saying "era siete años" is a common mistake from English; Spanish always uses tener for age.

Clock time in the past also uses the imperfect of ser. "Era la una" (It was one o'clock) uses the singular because una is one hour. For every other hour, use the plural: "Eran las ocho" (It was eight o'clock). The time does not start or end in the story; it is simply the setting.

Weather works the same way. "*Hacía* frío" (It was cold), "hacía sol" (it was sunny), "*llovía*" (it was raining) and "*nevaba*" (it was snowing) all describe the conditions. Put age, time and weather together and you have an opening line: "Eran las siete, hacía frío y yo tenía doce años." (It was seven, it was cold and I was twelve.)

words.d: had; with años, was (age) — Tenía diez años. (I/he/she was ten.)
it was (weather) — hacía calor, hacía frío, hacía viento
it was raining — imperfect of llover
it was snowing — imperfect of nevar

look.title: Example: Telling Time in the Past
look.cite: Example phrases; standard Spanish time expressions
look.prompt: Which hour is the only one that takes era instead of eran, and why?

check.q: How do you say "I was ten years old"?
check.why: Spanish uses tener for age, and background age in the past is imperfect: tenía.

check.q: "___ las tres cuando llegamos." Which form fits?
check.why: Time in the past uses the imperfect of ser, plural for every hour except one: eran las tres.

check.q: What does "Hacía mucho viento" mean?
choices: It made a lot of wind.
check.why: Hacía with weather words describes past weather: it was windy.

lessons.title: Cuando Era Niño o Niña
lessons.mainIdea: Cuando era niño or cuando era niña (when I was a child) opens a memory and sets up the imperfect.
reading: Many memories in Spanish begin with the same four words: "*Cuando era niña*..." or "Cuando era niño..." (When I was a child...). The ending matches the speaker: a girl or woman says niña, a boy or man says niño. Daniela's grandmother says, "Cuando era niña, vivía en Michoacán." (When I was a girl, I lived in Michoacán.)

The phrase sets a long stretch of time as the background. Everything that fits inside that stretch usually follows in the imperfect too. "Cuando era niño, mi familia tenía una tienda y yo ayudaba después de clases." (When I was a boy, my family had a store and I helped after school.) You can swap in other stages: cuando era joven (when I was young), cuando estaba en primaria (when I was in elementary school).

Michoacán is a state in western Mexico, and many families in Chicago have roots there. Memories are often shared at the table in more than one language. If your relatives mix Spanish and English, that is normal. The pattern still holds: cuando era niño or niña, then imperfect verbs that paint *la niñez* (childhood).

words.d: when I was a girl (a boy says cuando era niño)
childhood — En mi niñez... (In my childhood...)
young — cuando era joven (when I was young)
the memory — Tengo un recuerdo bonito. (I have a nice memory.)

look.title: Two Voices, One Pattern
look.text:
Abuela Rosa: Cuando era niña, dormía con mis dos hermanas en un cuarto pequeño.
Daniela: Cuando era niña, yo dormía con muchos peluches.
Abuela Rosa: ¿Y tu hermano?
Daniela: Cuando era niño, él tenía miedo de la oscuridad.
look.prompt: Start three sentences with cuando era niño or cuando era niña, and finish each with an imperfect verb.

check.q: A boy wants to say "When I was a child, I lived in Aurora." Which is correct?
choices: Cuando fui niño, viví en Aurora.
Cuando era niña, vivía en Aurora.
Cuando estaba niño, vivía en Aurora.
Cuando era niño, vivía en Aurora.
check.why: A boy says niño; the background of childhood uses era and vivía.

check.q: What does "Cuando era joven, mi abuela bailaba mucho" mean?
choices: When she is young, my grandmother will dance.
When she was young, my grandmother used to dance a lot.
My grandmother danced once when she was young.
check.why: Era joven sets the time, and bailaba describes a repeated habit.

check.q: Why does cuando era niña use ser and not estar?
choices: Being a child is a stage of life, described with ser.
Estar is only used in the present.
Ser is always used with cuando.
check.why: Stages of life like niño, joven and viejo describe what someone was, so they take ser.

lessons.title: Soler: Usually Did
lessons.mainIdea: Soler in the imperfect plus an infinitive means used to or usually did something.
reading: Spanish has a special verb for habits: *soler* (to usually do). It is always followed by an infinitive, the basic -ar, -er or -ir form of another verb. "Solía leer antes de dormir" means "I used to read before sleeping." Soler does the job of the habit, and leer names the action.

In the past, soler is almost always in the imperfect: solía, solías, solía, solíamos, solíais, solían. It is a regular -er verb here. "Mis padres solían cenar tarde." (My parents used to have dinner late.) Compare it with the plain imperfect: "Mis padres cenaban tarde." Both are correct and mean nearly the same thing. Solía simply puts a spotlight on the habit.

Two mistakes are common. First, conjugating both verbs: "solía leía." Only soler changes; the second verb stays an *infinitive* (the unconjugated form). Second, using soler for one event. "Ayer solía correr" does not make sense, because ayer (yesterday) is one day and soler means a habit.

words.d: to usually do — solía + infinitive: used to, usually did
the infinitive — a verb's basic form ending in -ar, -er or -ir (leer, jugar)
to have dinner — Solíamos cenar juntos. (We used to have dinner together.)

look.title: Two Ways to Say a Habit
look.text:
Plain imperfect: Los viernes, mi tío tocaba la guitarra.
With soler: Los viernes, mi tío solía tocar la guitarra.
(On Fridays, my uncle used to play the guitar.)
Only solía changes for the subject. Tocar stays the same.
look.prompt: Rewrite "Mi hermana corría en el parque" using solía. Which verb stays an infinitive?

check.q: Which sentence uses soler correctly?
check.why: Only soler is conjugated (solíamos); the second verb stays an infinitive: jugar.

check.q: What does "Mi abuela solía cantar en la cocina" mean?
choices: My grandmother sang once in the kitchen.
My grandmother is singing in the kitchen.
My grandmother wants to sing in the kitchen.
My grandmother used to sing in the kitchen.
check.why: Solía + infinitive describes a past habit: used to sing.

check.q: Why is "Ayer solía correr" wrong?
choices: Ayer is one day, but soler describes a repeated habit.
Ayer must go at the end.
check.why: Soler means usually do, so it cannot describe a single day like ayer.

lessons.title: Feelings and States in the Past
lessons.mainIdea: How someone felt or what they thought or wanted in the past is usually background, so it goes in the imperfect.
reading: Daniela asks, "¿Estabas contenta en tu pueblo?" (Were you happy in your town?) Her grandmother answers, "Sí, pero a veces *extrañaba* a mi papá cuando viajaba." (Yes, but sometimes I missed my dad when he traveled.) Feelings that lasted over time, like being happy or missing someone, are states, not events. Spanish puts them in the imperfect.

Verbs of thinking and wanting work the same way. "Pensaba que la ciudad era enorme" (I thought the city was huge). "Quería ser maestra" (I wanted to be a teacher). "No sabía leer" (I didn't know how to read). Estar with emotions is very common: estaba nerviosa, estaba cansado, estábamos *emocionados* (we were excited).

Watch for the English word "was." It can become era, estaba, fue or estuvo, depending on the meaning. For a feeling or condition in the background, estaba is usually right: "Estaba triste" (I was sad). Choosing fue for a feeling is a common error. Save the preterite for a feeling that began at a clear moment, which you will study in the next chapter.

words.d: to miss (someone or something) — Extrañaba mi pueblo. (I missed my town.)
excited — emocionada for a girl or woman; emocionados for a group
to want or love — imperfect: quería (I/he/she wanted)
to think — imperfect: pensaba (I/he/she thought)

look.title: Feelings on the First Day
look.text:
Mi primer día en Chicago, estaba muy nerviosa. No hablaba inglés y no conocía a nadie. Quería regresar a mi pueblo. Pero mi maestra era amable y sonreía mucho.
(My first day in Chicago, I was very nervous. I didn't speak English and I didn't know anyone. I wanted to go back to my town. But my teacher was kind and smiled a lot.)
look.prompt: Name the four feelings or states in the text. Then describe how you felt on a first day somewhere new.

check.q: "I was tired" as a background feeling. Which is best?
check.why: A temporary feeling uses estar, and as background it takes the imperfect: estaba cansado.

check.q: What does "No sabía nadar" mean?
choices: I didn't find out about swimming.
I won't know how to swim.
I didn't know how to swim.
check.why: Sabía is the imperfect of saber; with an infinitive it means knew how to.

check.q: Which sentence describes a lasting wish in the past?
check.why: Quería, the imperfect, describes a wish that lasted over time.

review.q: Which is the correct imperfect yo form of estudiar?
Which three verbs are irregular in the imperfect?
review.why: Only ser (era), ir (iba) and ver (veía) are irregular in the imperfect.

review.q: "Cuando ___ pequeños, mis hermanos y yo ___ en el río."
review.why: Childhood background (éramos) and a repeated habit (nadábamos) both take the imperfect.

review.q: "En el pueblo ___ tres escuelas." Which is standard?
review.why: Había stays singular even with a plural noun.
Solía + infinitive, with no preposition: solía comer.

review.q: How do you say "It was raining and it was cold"?
review.why: Weather background uses the imperfect: llovía, hacía frío. Lloraba means was crying.

review.q: Why does Abuela Rosa's whole memory use the imperfect?
choices: She is describing what life was like over many years.
She is talking about one single day.
The imperfect is used only by older speakers.
Spanish has only one past tense.
review.why: Habits and descriptions of a long stretch of time take the imperfect.

review.q: Which form has a written accent?
review.why: Every -ía form needs an accent on the í: veíamos.
